new_statements.second_reader_evidence: SIL Language & Culture Archives record 37413 (held text capture) lists the public PDF attachment, publisher LSNZ Auckland 1991, pp. 21-51: exists, open (bots get an automated-access block, humans a download). Held scan (32 pp., no text) at and Quote re-read at lines 287-289 and per-page scanned scanned/, AND checked against the page scan p. 27, sec. 2 'Standard Muna phonology', point 7): '7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked.' - verbatim. Identity: sec. 6 (the scanned textprinted p. 44) '4. Kioko (KIO) and Kambowa (KAMBO) on the east coast of Buton, on roughly the same line…
new_statements.relation_note: Penultimate stress, almost invariably, for Muna and all Munic/Pancanic isolects discussed including Kioko and Kambowa; no tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('almost invariably'), stated for Muna and asserted to hold equally for all other dialects and languages treated in the paper, among them Kioko (KIO) and Kambowa (KAMBO); stress is therefore left unmarked in the wordlist transcriptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in this paper (van den Berg 1989 reports secondary stress on the 4th and 6th syllables from the end for Muna only)
new_statements.exceptions: only the hedge 'almost invariably'; no exceptions specified here (the Muna grammar, van den Berg 1989 sec. 2.5-2.6, names certain vowel sequences and the clitic -a as the Muna exceptions; sec. 3g of this paper mentions Muna siua 'nine'-type forms only in van den Berg 2003).
new_statements.identity_note: ROUND1-REOPENED (round 1: print / not-attempted; opened here from the project's held mirror copy filed under sibling languoids liab1237/kaim1241, a scan downloaded earlier from the SIL archive via the Internet Archive, with existing tesseract scanned). The paper covers the Muna dialects plus the author's own wordlists of the 'Pancanic' isolects; sec. 6 p. 44 item 4: 'Kioko (KIO) and Kambowa (KAMBO) on the east coast of Buton, on roughly the same line as Raha. I did not visit these locations personally, but collected wordlists from speakers in Raha and Pure respectively.' KIO = Nuclear Kioko and KAMBO = Kambowa, i.e. both Glottolog dialects of kiok1239 [ues]. The stress statement is made for Muna and explicitly extended to 'the other dialects and languages to be discussed', which include KIO and KAMBO (their forms are cited in sec. 4-6, e.g. KIO kodo'o, konisi, fotaa; KAMBO moinipi, potaa).

sources.note: Not a Kioko source, but Mustopa & Abroor 2022 treat Kioko as a Muna dialect; if that identity is accepted the Muna grammar's stress statement is the nearest first-hand description. Only relevant with an explicit identity caveat.

sources.citation: Mead, David. 2020. Kambowa word list and notes. (Sulang Language Data and Working Papers: Word Lists, no. 9.) Sulawesi Language Alliance. 53 pp. Online:http://sulang.org/resources/word-lists/009
sources.note: No prose statement on stress, accent or tone anywhere in the 53 pp. (full-text search for stress/accent/penult/tone/pitch/prosod/tekanan: no hits; Section 4 'Sound system' read in full: phoneme inventory, syllable types V/CV/NCV, vowel sequences, marginal phonemes). The only prosodic information is implicit: every phonetic transcription in 4.2 carries the IPA stress mark on the penultimate vowel/mora ([kapaˈea], [buˈea], [ɓeˈau], [koˈie], [iˈoe], [raeˈao]; [ˈriː], [ˈneː], [ˈɗuː] for like-vowel sequences), consistent with penultimate stress counting vowels as syllables, but the author does not…

sources.citation: Mead, David. 2020. Kioko word list and notes. (Sulang Language Data and Working Papers: Word Lists, no. 10.) [s.l.]: Sulawesi Language Alliance. 40 pp. (SulangWordList010-v1; drafted 2012, published 5 March 2020; fieldwork Bonegunu, Buton Utara, 21 Nov 2000, 7-8 Sep 2012, 10 Nov 2019; respondents La'ua, Laiki A., Barahama, Sising).
sources.note: First-hand sketch of the sound system: 21 consonants /p t tʃ k ʔ ɓ ɗ (b d dʒ) g ɸ s χ h β m n ŋ (r) l/ + 5 vowels; open-syllable language (V, CV, NCV); notes on glottal stop, b/ɓ and d/ɗ distribution, *r > χ, χ~h merger in younger speakers. NO explicit statement of where word stress falls and nothing on tone. Stress evidence is indirect only: (i) the two phonetic transcriptions given carry initial = penultimate stress on disyllables ([ˈʔunto], [ˈʔeo]); (ii) one loanword in the 844-item list is written with a stress mark, ˈdanau 'lake' 'from Malay' (the only stress-marked list entry, i.e. flag…

sources.citation: Susiati. 2020. Dialektometri segitiga: Hubungan kekerabatan bahasa di Sulawesi Tenggara (Bahasa Wakatobi, Bahasa Cia-Cia, Bahasa Pancana, Bahasa Kioko, Bahasa Tolaki). OSF preprint, 18 pp. DOI 10.31219/osf.io/bjpxm (Glottolog ref 668132).
sources.note: Nothing. Lexicostatistic dialectometry over Swadesh-type lists (Kioko collected in Kabupaten Buton Utara); the only occurrences of 'aksen'/'fonologi' are generic definitions in the introduction (pp. 3-4). Finds Pancana vs Kioko at 31-50% = 'subdialect' difference. No stress, no 'tekanan'.

sources.citation: La Ino. 2016. The reconstruction of protolanguage Muna and Kambowa. International Journal of Linguistics, Literature and Culture (IJLLC) 2(3): 151-168 (Crossref: pp. 125ff, DOI 10.21744/ijllc.v2i3.265). Faculty of Humanities, Halu Oleo University, Kendari.
sources.note: Phonology content = segmental inventories only: Table 3 'Vowels of Kambowa' (i e a o u), Table 4 'Consonants of Kambowa' (23 consonants incl. implosive, prenasalised mp mb nt nd ns ŋk ŋg), then PAN > Proto-Muna-Kambowa sound correspondences (apocope of final C, etc.) and lexicostatistic tables. No mention of stress, accent, tekanan, syllable weight or tone anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing for stress/accent/tekanan/penult/tone). Cites 'La Ino 2015' (unpublished/seminar version, Padang) as the data source.

sources.citation: Mead, David. 2003. Evidence for a Celebic supergroup. In John Lynch (ed.), Issues in Austronesian historical phonology, 115-141. (Pacific Linguistics 550.) Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University.
sources.note: Nothing about Kioko prosody. Kioko appears ~39 times as segmental cognate data (x < *r, loss of *q, etc.); the single occurrence of 'word stress' concerns the unexplained conditioning of the PMP *s > s/h split across South-eastern Celebic, not stress placement in any language. No tone.

sources.citation: van den Berg, René. 2003. The place of Tukang Besi and the Muna-Buton languages. In John Lynch (ed.), Issues in Austronesian historical phonology, 87-113. (Pacific Linguistics 550.) Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-550.87
sources.note: No Kioko phonology. Reconstructs Proto-Muna-Buton phonology incl. point 10 'Stress was penultimate.' (p. 96) and notes Muna siua 'nine' keeps antepenultimate stress (p. 92); these are statements about the proto-language and Muna, not about Kioko, which is merely listed as a Munic language.
